# Baiame at work: forestry, conservation & outdoor industries, environmental & climate services, and the myths that got there first

The myths did not retire. They moved offices. This is the file on where **Baiame** works now.

Baiame's mythology is preserved in the oral traditions of the Wiradjuri, Gamilaraay, and neighbouring nations. The stories are not free-floating entertainment: they are title deeds to country, instruction manuals for law, and maps of the sky. What follows are widely reported themes; local elders hold the authoritative versions of each nation's stories.

The [pattern atlas](/patterns/) — which maps every flagship temple to the industries its archetype demonstrably resonates with, each match argued and open to challenge — seats this temple in **6 industries**. This file reads those seats the way they were earned: through the myths.

## At a Glance

- **Temple:** Baiame
- **Pantheon:** Aboriginal
- **Domain of influence:** Sky Father, Creator
- **Pattern seats:** 6
- **Sectors touched:** Energy & Natural World · Commerce & Governance · Culture & Entertainment
- **Strongest seat:** Forestry, Conservation & Outdoor Industries
- **Series:** The Resonance Files, No. 63 of 449

## The Myth at Work

**The Making of the World.** In the beginning Baiame shaped the land.  He formed the hills and rivers, planted the trees, and made the animals. — hold that image; the industries below are where it goes to work.

**The Retreat to the Sky.** When the work of creation was finished, Baiame rose into the sky and made his camp there.  From that distant place he watches over the world he made. — that is not just a story. It is a business model, four thousand years early.

## The Long Employment

Baiame remains a powerful symbol of Aboriginal sovereignty over country and culture.  His name appears in place names, in rock art and stencil sites, and in contemporary Aboriginal art and literature. The age changed. The work did not.
